sourceInformation.source: Kaboom! (1981), an arcade bomb-catching game by Activision for the Atari 2600
sourceInformation.perspective: Fixed orthographic side view of a 3D rooftop (2.5D)
sourceInformation.tech: Three.js 0.180.0 (r180), WebGPURenderer with WebGL 2 compatibility fallback; Rapier 0.19.3; Gamepad API; Web Audio API; WebRTC; AI Hub session client 1.4.0 / protocol v1; esbuild 0.25.11
sourceInformation.artDirection: Procedural cel-shaded 3D diorama, inverted ink outlines, warm printed-paper palette and comic typography
sourceInformation.animation: Three.js AnimationMixer, AnimationClip and native keyframe tracks for character, bird and catch animations; procedural physics and particles
sourceInformation.audio: Code-only Web Audio music, sound effects and formant-synthesized Animalese-style gibberish voices. Music defaults to 10%
sourceInformation.online: AI Hub ghost score races for 1–4 players; standalone direct WebRTC score race for 2 players with manual invite/reply codes; local 2-player co-op
sourceInformation.testing: 38/38 automated checks passed, including a full six-shift Rapier playthrough, emulated standard gamepad, touch, Web Audio signal, actual two-page WebRTC pairing/results, WebKit and renderer recovery. AI Hub passed 45 protocol assertions across 2-player, 4-player with 150 ms latency / 50 ms jitter / 5% loss, and host-departure scenarios. Screenshots inspected at 1920×1080 and portrait mobile. Physical-controller feel, real mobile hardware and subjective audio quality: unknown.
sourceInformation.research: None. Used native model knowledge; downloaded requested libraries and the supplied AI Hub integration contract only

testingFeedback: 8 distinct game issues were found through scripted tests, visual inspection and test-driven review: accumulating wind, low-contrast HUD text, hidden-overlay CSS precedence, invalid font declarations, renderer resource lifecycle, controller scrolling in credits, overlapping portrait HUD controls and online difficulty changing through settings. All were corrected. Timing/readback problems in the headless test setup were tracked separately.

3 were potentially game breaking: wind made later shifts impossible, the hidden loading overlay blocked clicks, and renderer lifecycle errors could stop drawing after a restart or backend change. All were corrected.
The complete six-shift Rapier playthrough. It exposed persistent wind-force accumulation at shift three; the corrected run caught all 184 deliveries and completed every shift.
Headless WebGPU pixel readback. Software-driver and readback failures made it unreliable visual evidence. Renderer submission state and compatibility-backend screenshots were more useful.
engineFeedback: Native AnimationMixer tracks, procedural geometry and toon node materials let character motion, water tubs and the illustrated rooftop share one scene. Rapier sensor events made catches precise.

I first treated persistent Rapier forces as per-step forces, which accumulated wind. I also encountered renderer cache/lifecycle problems while reusing or disposing compiled resources, and unreliable software WebGPU readback. Fresh scene resources and guarded startup/recovery resolved the application issues.
The catch/combo/douse/wave state machine, controller-first shared UI, touch assistance, procedural sound and both multiplayer lifecycles.
Coordinating asynchronous GPU initialization and recovery with physics, native animation, input and network round start/end, while keeping the single-file game usable offline.
None to engine source. Used stock Three.js 0.180.0 and Rapier 0.19.3; recovery and compatibility handling live in the application.
A documented device-loss recovery API that replaces a renderer without invalidating node materials or leaving pending compilation work.
promptFeedback: The concrete source, controller-first brief, code-only audio and single-file delivery made the creative target clear.
The ban on research alongside a required online integration reference needed interpretation. I fetched that contract and dependency code directly as implementation material, without web research.
Making polished gameplay, all input types, the attract loop, live developer controls, self-contained packaging and two online lifecycles work as one coherent game.
Clarify the expected standalone online pairing flow and whether TURN relay or matchmaking infrastructure is provided, or manual serverless WebRTC pairing is sufficient.

aiHub.name: Ka-Whoosh!
aiHub.tagline: A little panic. A lot of splash.
aiHub.description: A masked rooftop rascal is raining trouble. Slide your stack of water tubs, nail perfect catches and unleash an emergency douse across six escalating shifts, solo, in couch co-op or in an online score race.
aiHub.controls: Move: left stick / D-pad, A-D / arrows, mouse or drag; douse: Cross / A, Space, click or second touch; pause: Options / Escape. Local P2: arrows and Enter, or second gamepad.
